en: Homage to the illustrious Vajranātha! I shall proclaim the *Sahajasiddhi*, the Accomplishment of the Innate, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
It transcends the fire-oblation sacrifice and is free from the rituals of beginners. ||1||
The true nature of the innate reality (sahajavastu) is called the accomplishment of peace (sāntisiddhi);
therefore, the innate (sahaja) is known as the accomplishment of the innate (sahajasiddhi), which is inexpressible. ||2||

And having meditated on the bhaga within the element of space, one should perform the meditation in the center, preceded by the wheel, according to the rule and according to the arising of the deities. ||3||
Regarding the phrase "in the element of space": "lotus" is known as gnosis, and "vagina" (bhaga) is so remembered.
"Meditation" (bhāvanā) is meditative absorption (samāpatti), and its bliss is called the "wheel" (cakra). ||4||
The bodhicitta, which is to be personally realized according to the proper method, arises as the deity; it is twofold emptiness, abiding as the innate (*sahaja*). ||5||
Wisdom is said to be the woman, while skillful means is remembered as the man;
subsequently, there is a twofold division of these two according to the distinction between the ultimate (vivṛti) and the conventional (saṃvṛti). ||6||
First, there is a twofold nature in the male: either semen or his pleasure;
and just as it is with the male, so it is with regard to wisdom—either semen or his pleasure.
For this very reason, Ānanda, because of the fourfold classification, the innate [nature] is of four kinds, as it was taught by the Perfectly Awakened One. (8)
Through Ānanda there is some pleasure; Paramānanda is superior to that.
Viramānanda is the state of detachment, while Sahajānanda remains as the remainder. ||9||
The first is the longing for touch; the second is the awakening of pleasure;
the third is the destruction of passion; by that, the fourth is so described. ||10||
In the first stage, wisdom becomes warm; in the second, it becomes like smoke;
in the third, it emits sparks; and in the fourth, it blazes forth like fire. ||11||
The Caṇḍālī blazes at the navel and burns the five Tathāgatas; she burns Locanā and the others, and once they are burnt, the moon (HAM) flows forth. 12.
Just as the two-fold nature of the bodhicitta was previously established by the Victors, so too should it be understood here in the union with the wisdom-vajra. (13)
Form, sound, as well as smell, taste, and likewise touch,
and that which has the nature of the dharma-realm— just as one practices with envy, so too should joy be seen in each individual sense-base, four by four. (14)
The innate nature is not described by another, nor is it found in anyone else;
it is known by oneself through the service of awakening and a virtuous guru. 15.
In the *Sahajasiddhi* composed by the venerable Śrīḍombiheruka, the first chapter is the "Instruction on the Innate.
Whether they be inferior, middling, or superior, and whatever others there may be—all these should be seen as equal through the meditations on reality (*tattva*). (1)
That which is inferior is the subtle object, while the superior is said to be the state of being; that which is intermediate is devoid of both—these others are the six sense-faculties. (2)
Those which are stable and moving are the deficient arts; those which are equal have identical activity, being of one flavor through the cultivation of reality. (3)
It is said that "equal" means "identical," and that is remembered as being of a single flavor (*ekarasa*).
By this meaning, it is called "of equal flavor" (*samarasa*) and "of a single nature" (*ekabhāvya*). ||4||
In this world, one should resort to five families;
through service to these families, there arises auspicious accomplishment that grants all desires.
(3) Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasaṃbhava, and the Lord Bhūpati...
And likewise, it is proclaimed as "Amogha" (Unfailing) for the sake of the accomplishment of sentient beings. ||6||
Akṣobhya is said to be the vajra, and Amitābha is indeed the lotus;
Ratnasaṃbhava is the jewel, and likewise Vairocana is the Tathāgata. (7)
It is said that action is unfailing; one should condense these families.
Success comes from the service of the family—this was spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One. (8)
In this world, those who are terrified do not take pleasure in the families beginning with the letter *ha*;
for instruction given to the deluded leads only to provocation, not to peace.
Hevajra is known through that, either by faith or when there is hearing;
it is concealed from unfortunate beings and is told to those who are fortunate. ||10||
The commitments (samayas) that are to be observed have been set at ten in number;
due to their division into two kinds based on their innate nature (sahaja), they are five each, distinct from one another. ||11||
Beginning with *ga* or beginning with *ha*, ending with the middle or beginning with the first;
[the syllable] *na*, or one [syllable] out of fear, or hidden due to worldly convention. (12)
Externally, they will be known as Tathāgatas through the distinction of colors: black, white, red, and dark-yellow. (13)
For the entire world—namely, the three realms—is indeed conjoined with the co-emergent (sahaja);
by that very [co-emergent] all is pervaded, O you who drink the world. 14.
Thinking thus, the yogi of great intelligence reflects: "I am certainly such as this," and experiences the supreme bliss like that of innate joy. (4) 15.
Whether eating, drinking, bathing, awake, or even in sleep, one should contemplate this constantly; thereby, those who desire the state of bliss attain it. (16)
The second [chapter], the Instruction on the Reality of the Samaya, in the *Sahajasiddhi* composed by the venerable ŚrīḌombiheruka. III.
As it has been said: "And that which is external, in the practice of the Samayamathavatā" (or *Samayamatatattvopadeśa*).
In the Hevajrayoginītantra, that of the Hero is described afterwards. ||1||
May Brahmā protect those who are pure here and there;
one must always practice purity, not through the mere recitation of words.
They grieve for merit and knowledge, or for the bliss that is personally experienced;
purity consists in the nature of personal experience, and one is not liberated by any other kind of purity. //3//
That practice is shown to be performed by one who is enveloped by the Veda and the non-Veda;
it is remembered that for those who serve, that practice is to be carried out through service. ||4||

Even a disciple who has attained spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*) shall not fail to prostrate before the Guru; for by transgressing the Guru’s word, one may instantly fall even into the Avīci hell and other such realms. (5) Indeed, the entire world is conceptualized by the mind—that which is not conceptualized by the mind does not exist.
The thorough knowledge of all phenomena is cultivation; indeed, it is not cultivation at all. //6//
Whatever beings there are, whether stable or moving— creepers, shrubs, grasses, and so forth—
one should indeed contemplate the supreme reality, which is the very nature of the self.
For them, there is no supreme [attainment] here other than self-cognized great bliss;
for accomplishment is self-cognized, and indeed meditation is self-cognized. //8//
Action consists of self-awareness, and from it arises the action of meditative cultivation;
one is oneself the agent, oneself the remover, oneself the king, and oneself the sovereign.
In the same way, passion, hatred, envy, delusion, and pride—these five afflictions are to be seen as arising from the great bliss of the King of Knowledge. (10)
Even though it has been consumed...
[then] they go to Sukhāvatī; Siddhavīra, the Great Bliss, abides in every aspect, relying upon the ultimate reality (paramārtha). ||12||
At the time of accomplishment, one becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*):
divine sight, divine hearing, divine smell, divine touch, and divine taste; and with a divine body and mind, one is endowed with enjoyment while remaining in another place.
The third chapter: The Instruction on the Determination of the Accomplishment of the Samaya, within the *Sahajasiddhi* composed by the venerable ŚrīḌombiheruka.
The *Sahajasiddhi*, composed by the venerable master ŚrīḌombiheruka, is completed.
